b: In September 2026, the New York Times published an article titled “30 Ideas for Fixing US Schools, Ranked by Experts” to address the problem of declining literacy and math rates across the United States. The experts identified solutions based on effectiveness and relative cost, highlighting the top five solutions as small reading groups, science of reading, universal pre-K, increased funding, and increased teacher pay for under-resourced schools and communities.
To be clear, these ideas are backed by science and arguably would be welcomed policy changes for supporting U.S. students.
But even these interventions on their own will continue to fail students if we don’t address the bigger underlying concern: Schools were never designed for children’s development.

The model of our public education system was informed by an 18th-century Prussian military regime with the intended goal of preparing students for work in factories. The United States, deep into the Industrial Revolution, needed workers who could follow instructions, keep a schedule, and perform quality work. U.S. public schools were a solution to overcrowded, one-room schoolhouses and the need to support a new workforce.

It’s no wonder then that reform efforts date back literally to the inception of public education itself. While lots of positive changes have come from those efforts, including accommodations for students with disabilities and scientific advancements in how to educate, the problem persists: Schools don’t align with child development.
The research is clear on what works for children, especially young learners from preschool through eight years of age. Children learn best:

When they are in play. Play is their language, their work. It is where they learn to compromise and persuade. Where they make sense out of life and learn about themselves. It is where they explore new concepts and make them their own. Academics are not separate from play. Indeed, play is the epicenter of children’s learning networks.

When they are moving their bodies. Science is firm on this—when children learn a new concept and then move their bodies freely (unstructured play—not just doing a couple of yoga moves at their desk), their brains metabolize the new idea into long-term memory. Plus, children are not designed to sit still for long periods of time. The rule of thumb is three minutes per year old. So that 8-year-old? Twenty-four minutes, tops. Five-year-old? Fifteen minutes. You can force them to sit longer, but the trade-off is that their cognitive energy is now focused on staying seated, not the instruction itself.

When they have short bursts of instruction. Cognitive science has said this for over six decades now: short bursts of learning followed by movement throughout the day yield a dramatic increase in long-term learning compared to longer learning sessions. It feels counter-intuitive to today’s narrative that more is better. Kids are behind? Cram more learning into the day. But that is not how our kids’ brains work. Do less to learn more.

When they are in multi-age groupings. A significant body of literature has shown the benefits of children being in multi-age groups, as opposed to the current standard of grade levels. Children benefit from older student role models; older students learn compassion and patience supporting younger students. Watch kids at the playground or around family gatherings and you will see this dynamic. It’s intrinsic and yet our current system removes this dynamic from their world.

When they can lean on their intrinsic curiosity for understanding how the world works, not learn to a test. Children are born curious! They not only want to learn, but are hard-wired to make connections, test assumptions, and revise what they used to think. Yet when we tell them how to think, what to think, and what is considered “right,” we quickly extinguish the love of learning from them.

The harsh reality is that when developmentally appropriate practice is stripped from education, then all the best curricula in the world will have minimal effects, at best. The list of 30 best ideas for fixing U.S. public schools? That is phase 2.

We must begin with the root cause of the challenges we are seeing. The kids are letting us know in no uncertain terms that they are done with the 18th-century structure that wasn’t even designed for them in the first place.

Put child development experts at the helm. Reimagine public education from the ground up for kids, not in spite. When we let them learn from a developmental perspective, then we leverage the innate gifts and talents our children already have. They want to learn. They have the capacity to think deeply and creatively. The problem is that we have removed every ounce of developmentally appropriate learning from the schools. And then we wonder why it isn’t working.
Transform the environment. Bring in child development research to guide the way. That is where we begin. That is where we will find the solutions.
